title: Food & Drink
description: What's on the plate and in the glass at a warung, and the words for how it tastes: pedas, manis, enak.

items.pitfallNote: Nasi is cooked rice only. Uncooked rice in a shop is beras, and rice growing in the field is padi.
items.cultureNote: Many Indonesians feel they haven't really eaten until they've had rice, however big the snack before it.

items.registerNotes: Menus usually spell it mie: mie goreng (fried noodles), mie ayam (chicken noodles). Mi is the standard spelling.
One word for the bird and the meat. Ayam penyet or ayam geprek, fried chicken smashed into sambal, is a warung favourite.

items.cultureNote: At seafood stalls by the sea you often pick your fish, pay by weight and have it grilled as ikan bakar.

items.registerNotes: Name the animal after it: daging sapi (beef), daging kambing (goat, often called mutton on menus), daging babi (pork).
items.cultureNote: Most Indonesians are Muslim and don't eat pork, so babi is rare outside Bali, Chinese restaurants and some Christian regions.

items.registerNotes: Also a dish of vegetables, often in broth: sayur asem, sayur lodeh.

items.pitfallNote: Buah is also the counter for things (dua buah tas, two bags), so you'll meet it far from the fruit stall.

items.registerNotes: At a warung: telur ceplok (fried egg), telur dadar (omelette), telur rebus (boiled egg). Often said and written telor.
Comes with almost every meal. To have it on the side, ask Sambalnya dipisah, ya.
items.pitfallNote: Many sambals contain shrimp paste (terasi). If you're vegetarian or allergic, ask Ada terasinya?
Pedas is chilli-hot; hot in temperature is panas. Jangan terlalu pedas, ya means not too spicy, please.
items.cultureNote: Not spicy to the cook can still be spicy to you. Tidak pakai cabai (no chilli) is the safe request.

items.registerNotes: Drinks come sweet unless you ask: es teh manis is the standard iced tea. Said of a person, manis means sweet-looking, attractive.
Ikan asin, salted dried fish, is a common side dish. Too salty is terlalu asin.
The everyday way to praise food: Enak sekali (it's delicious). It also means pleasant in general: Enak di sini (it's nice here).
items.pitfallNote: Saya tidak enak badan means I'm not feeling well. In casual speech, nggak enak can also mean feeling awkward or bad about something.

items.registerNotes: Served sweet by default. Ask for teh tawar for no sugar; teh hangat is warm tea, es teh iced tea.
Kopi hitam is black coffee; kopi susu has milk, often sweetened condensed milk.
items.cultureNote: Warung coffee is often kopi tubruk: the grounds settle at the bottom of the glass, so leave the last mouthful.

items.pitfallNote: Air alone is any water, including tap water. To drink, ask for air putih (literally white water); bottled water is air mineral.
items.cultureNote: Tap water isn't for drinking in Indonesia. Air putih at a warung or a home is boiled or filtered.

items.registerNotes: Before a drink, es makes it iced: es teh, es jeruk (iced orange juice). Pakai es? means with ice?, and tidak pakai es is no ice.
To cut down: Gulanya sedikit saja (just a little sugar) or Tidak pakai gula (no sugar). Gula merah or gula Jawa is palm sugar.
Sepiring is a plateful. A bowl is a mangkuk.
items.cultureNote: Indonesians eat with a spoon in the right hand and a fork in the left, or with the right hand alone. Knives are rarely used.

items.registerNotes: After the food in dish names: nasi goreng, ayam goreng, pisang goreng (banana fritters). Grilled is bakar: ayam bakar, ikan bakar.
